## Why the answer is 6.2.1 and not what the repo pinned

The manifest review turned up a conflict I did **not** install blindly:

| file | pinned `tar` |
|---|---|
| `package.json` | `^6.2.0` (range) |
| **`npm-shrinkwrap.json`** | **`6.2.0`** ← wins over package-lock |
| `package-lock.json` | `6.2.1` |

`npm install --dry-run` confirmed a plain install resolves to **6.2.0**, which the registry itself marks deprecated: *"contain widely publicized security vulnerabilities, which have been fixed in the current version."* I diffed the two tarballs from the mirror — the only functional change in 6.2.1 is the new `maxDepth` guard in `lib/unpack.js` that rejects excessively deep entry paths. Since this tool untars archives from **external senders** into the ingest staging area, installing the vulnerable extractor was the one thing not to do here.

So I updated `npm-shrinkwrap.json`'s `tar` entry to `6.2.1` (the value `package-lock.json` already carried, still inside `^6.2.0`), then ran `npm install`. That is the only file I changed:
```
 M vendor/import-cli/npm-shrinkwrap.json
```
Verification after install: `npm ls` → `tar@6.2.1`; the installed tree is byte-identical to the genuine `tar-6.2.1.tgz` (sha1 `717549c5…`, sha512 `DZ4yORTwrbTj…` — matches both lockfiles and registry metadata, so the mirror is serving untampered packages); no `install`/`postinstall` hooks in any of the 9 installed packages; `npm ci --dry-run` passes, so CI stays green.

## Recommendations (not applied — your call)
1. **Commit the shrinkwrap bump**, otherwise the next `npm install` on a clean checkout reinstalls 6.2.0.
2. Consider raising the floor in `package.json` to `^6.2.1` so a lockless resolve can never pick 6.2.0 again.
3. `.npmrc` sets `audit=false`, which is why nothing warned about the vulnerable pin — worth enabling for this integration, or adding a CI gate on the shrinkwrap.
4. The sample archive itself is clean (3 regular files under `incoming-batch/`, no `..` traversal, no symlinks), so this run had no exposure even on the older version — but real partner batches are untrusted input.
